subtopic: Mental Health Act - assessment vs treatment order
subtopic_detail: Threshold and duration for initial assessment authority
stem:
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after neighbours called about him shouting at his upstairs windows and refusing to come out. On arrival he tells you strangers are pumping gas into his flat and that he has not slept for four nights. He declines admission, says nothing is wrong, and asks to leave.

He has no known previous psychiatric contact and no collateral is available beyond the police narrative. You are the ED registrar and consider that he meets criteria for detention under the state Mental Health Act but you have not yet been able to establish a diagnosis or a full treatment plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 148/92, RR 20, SpO2 99% on air, temperature 37.0.
data_table.Examination: Vigilant, pressured speech, persecutory content, no fluctuating attention, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: VBG, UEC, LFTs, urine drug screen sent and pending.

lead_in: Which authorisation under the state Mental Health Act is most appropriate at this point?

options.text: An assessment order to authorise detention for further psychiatric examination and initial observation
options.rationale: Australian state Mental Health Acts share a two-stage model: an assessment order (or equivalent) is the initial short-duration authority used when a person appears to have a mental illness or disorder, requires assessment, and is refusing voluntary engagement. It permits detention and examination but not compulsory treatment beyond what is immediately necessary. The duration is time-limited (typically hours to days depending on jurisdiction) and must be reviewed before conversion. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022; RANZCP Code of Ethics).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

options.text: A treatment order to authorise commencement of antipsychotic medication in the ED without full assessment
options.rationale: Treatment orders across state Acts require prior assessment establishing a mental illness meeting statutory criteria and a considered treatment plan by an authorised psychiatrist. A treatment order cannot be the initial instrument when assessment is incomplete. Would premature and outside statutory pathway. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: A community treatment order to require outpatient follow-up and depot medication after discharge home
options.rationale: A CTO applies to a person already assessed and typically transitioning from inpatient care; it cannot be used to authorise initial ED detention or replace acute assessment authority. Would misapply the instrument. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

options.text: Reliance on the common-law doctrine of emergency necessity to hold him without any statutory order at all
options.rationale: Common-law necessity may cover brief acute steps but every Australian state provides a specific statutory pathway that must be used once a mental health emergency is recognised. Would be legally weaker than the available Act. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics 2018).

options.text: Discharge home with a documented request that police return him if his behaviour deteriorates further overnight
options.rationale: The clinical picture meets the least-restrictive threshold for detention for assessment and discharging shifts risk to third parties without addressing an apparent mental illness with risk features. Would be unsafe and inconsistent with duty of care. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

explanation.summary: State Mental Health Acts distinguish assessment orders (short, permit detention for examination) from treatment orders (longer, permit compulsory treatment after assessment). The correct instrument in the ED when a person appears mentally unwell but has not yet been fully assessed is the assessment order.
key_points: Assessment order authorises detention for examination, not routine treatment
Treatment orders require prior authorised-psychiatrist assessment
CTOs are outpatient instruments after acute care
Common-law necessity is a stop-gap, not a substitute for statutory pathway
Duration is jurisdiction-specific but always time-limited with review
explanation.pearls: The Act is designed to be used in sequence: assessment order first, then treatment order if the criteria and treatment plan are established.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

stem:
A 27-year-old woman with a documented diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder presents to your community mental health clinic. She has stopped her aripiprazole depot 6 weeks ago. She reports thoughts that her upstairs neighbour is monitoring her but is not distressed and is not acting on the belief. She agrees to restart her depot today, accepts a home-visit tomorrow from her case manager, and her mother (with whom she lives) is present and offering support and observation.

She has no current suicidal ideation, no plans to harm the neighbour, and no history of acting on similar beliefs during previous episodes. You consider whether to complete a state Mental Health Act assessment order.

data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged, mildly guarded, no thought disorder, no command hallucinations elicited.
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative; recent bloods within normal limits.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Complete an assessment order under the state Act and arrange inpatient admission for stabilisation of her illness
options.rationale: The least-restrictive-alternative principle prohibits involuntary admission when voluntary community treatment is genuinely available and adequate. Would breach a statutory criterion. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Restart the depot today, arrange the case-manager home visit, and continue voluntary community management
options.rationale: State Mental Health Acts require that involuntary detention be used only when there is no less-restrictive alternative that would adequately address the risk. This patient meets the mental-illness limb but not the risk-plus-no-alternative limb: she is accepting treatment, has family observation, has no acute risk features, and a viable outpatient plan exists. Voluntary community management is legally and ethically indicated. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007 s 12; RANZCP Code of Ethics).

options.text: Complete a community treatment order to compel ongoing depot administration and outpatient case-management supervision
options.rationale: A CTO also requires that no less-restrictive alternative exists. When the patient is presently accepting treatment voluntarily a CTO cannot be justified as necessary. Would not meet threshold. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

options.text: Defer the depot until psychiatrist review next week and manage supportively with family observation only
options.rationale: Delaying resumption of maintenance treatment prolongs the relapse trajectory when the patient is willing and able to receive it today. Would be clinically inferior. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics 2018).

options.text: Notify police of a potential threat to the neighbour and document a duty-to-warn discharge from clinic today
options.rationale: There is no articulated threat, no plan, and no history of acting on similar beliefs; duty-to-warn thresholds are not met and the disclosure would breach confidentiality. Would be a category error. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

explanation.summary: Involuntary detention under state Mental Health Acts requires all limbs to be satisfied: mental illness or disorder, risk of serious harm to self or others or serious deterioration, AND no less-restrictive alternative. Failing the third limb is the most common lawful reason to keep a patient voluntary despite ongoing illness.
key_points: All limbs of the involuntary criteria must be satisfied
Presence of illness alone is insufficient
Willingness to accept treatment collapses the no-alternative limb
Family support is an alternative-forming factor
Deferring effective treatment is not a least-restrictive alternative
explanation.pearls: The Act is a floor for civil liberties, not a ceiling for clinical concern. If a voluntary plan is genuinely workable, it is required.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

stem:
A 78-year-old man is admitted with a wet gangrenous right forefoot on a background of type 2 diabetes and peripheral vascular disease. The vascular team recommends a below-knee amputation given failed revascularisation. He tells you he understands he could die of infection if he refuses, describes the operation as 'cutting my leg off below the knee', but insists that he would rather die intact than live as an amputee. His daughter says he has always felt this way.

He has a mild vascular cognitive impairment (MoCA 24/30) but is oriented, not delirious, and consistent across two conversations 24 hours apart. The surgical team asks you to determine whether he has decision-making capacity to refuse surgery.

data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs within normal limits; CRP 180; delirium screen negative on both reviews.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly supports the conclusion that he has capacity to refuse the amputation?

options.text: The presence of a mildly abnormal MoCA score above the standard impairment cut-off used for cognitive screening
options.rationale: Corroboration of preference is useful context but does not itself establish that the patient can currently understand, retain, weigh and communicate. Would be supportive but not the direct test. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines).

options.text: His daughter confirms this refusal is consistent with his lifelong values around bodily integrity and disability
options.rationale: MoCA measures cognition, not decisional capacity; capacity is decision-specific and functional. A normal cognitive screen neither confirms nor excludes capacity for a given decision. Would confuse a cognitive test with a functional assessment. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines).

options.text: He can weigh the risks of death from sepsis against his own valuation of body integrity and communicate a stable choice
options.rationale: Australian and international consensus (the MacCAT-T framework and NHMRC consent guidance) tests capacity across four functional abilities: understand information relevant to the decision, retain it, weigh it in the balance to arrive at a decision, and communicate the decision. Weighing includes applying the person's own values, and the stability of the decision on repeat interview supports authentic weighing rather than an impulsive or distorted judgement. (Source: NHMRC General Guidelines for Medical Practitioners on Providing Information to Patients; Grisso and Appelbaum MacCAT-T).

options.text: He describes the proposed operation accurately in lay terms and can restate the surgical plan on repeat questioning
options.rationale: Accurate description shows understanding, one of four limbs; capacity requires the weighing limb in particular, which is where refusal cases most often turn. Would be necessary but not sufficient. (Source: MacCAT-T).

options.text: He is oriented to time, place and person and shows no signs of delirium on repeat bedside cognitive screening
options.rationale: Absence of delirium removes an obscuring factor but does not itself demonstrate the four functional abilities that constitute capacity. Would clear a hurdle rather than pass the test. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision-specific and functional. The four abilities (understand, retain, weigh, communicate) must all be present. Weighing is the limb most often at stake in refusal-of-treatment cases and includes applying the patient's own values coherently.
key_points: Capacity is decision-specific, not global
Cognitive test scores do not establish or refute capacity
All four functional abilities must be present
Consistency on repeat interview supports authentic weighing
Values-based refusal is not evidence of incapacity
explanation.pearls: An unwise decision is not an incapable decision. The threshold turns on process, not outcome.

subtopic_detail: Consent for admission does not equal consent for medication
stem:
A 45-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder is admitted voluntarily to a mental health unit for a manic episode after discussion with her outpatient psychiatrist. She signs the voluntary admission form and settles on the ward overnight. The next morning the treating team wants to commence olanzapine 10 mg orally. She reads the medication information sheet, tells the team she does not want any medication and would prefer to try to sleep more and 'ride it out', and reiterates that she is happy to remain on the ward for observation.

She describes the risks of untreated mania, recognises she is unwell, and is coherent. She has capacity assessed to be intact for this decision.

data_table.Examination: Elevated mood, mildly pressured speech, no psychotic features, sleeping 3 hours per night.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Administer the olanzapine now because her voluntary admission implies broader consent to routine inpatient ward treatment
options.rationale: Voluntary admission for observation remains clinically appropriate and she is willing; discharge would be a punitive response to a lawful refusal. Would be inconsistent with duty of care. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

options.text: Convert her to involuntary status under the state Mental Health Act so that oral medication can be commenced today
options.rationale: Voluntary admission does not import consent to specific drug therapy; that would render the second consent conversation meaningless. Would breach the informed-consent standard. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines).

options.text: Discharge her from the ward this morning given that she has declined the specific medication that was proposed
options.rationale: Involuntary status requires satisfaction of statutory criteria including no less-restrictive alternative; simple treatment refusal by a person with capacity who is engaging with observation does not meet threshold. Would misuse the Act. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Withhold the olanzapine and continue observation, with a documented plan to reassess if her mental state or capacity changes
options.rationale: Voluntary admission provides consent to be on the ward and to nursing observation; it does NOT constitute blanket consent to psychotropic medication. Each treatment requires its own informed consent from a person with capacity. Where capacity is intact and the patient declines a specific medication, that refusal must be respected while continuing safe supportive care, with reassessment as the clinical picture evolves. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines; RANZCP Code of Ethics 2018).

options.text: Administer the olanzapine covertly in her breakfast to prevent further clinical deterioration while she remains on the ward
options.rationale: Covert medication in a person with capacity is a battery and breaches multiple ethical obligations; it is never justified where capacity is intact and refusal is documented. Would be unlawful. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

explanation.summary: Consent to admission and consent to specific treatments are separate. A voluntary inpatient with capacity may refuse individual interventions, and that refusal must be respected while continuing appropriate supportive care.
key_points: Voluntary admission is not consent to medication
Each treatment needs its own informed consent
Refusal by a capacitous patient must be documented and respected
Involuntary status is not a workaround for treatment refusal
Covert medication is not justified where capacity is intact
explanation.pearls: If the patient later loses capacity or meets statutory criteria the situation changes. Capacity must be reassessed at that point, not assumed backward.

stem:
A 32-year-old man with a 10-year history of paranoid schizophrenia has had three inpatient admissions in the last 18 months. Each admission has followed him stopping oral risperidone in the community, becoming acutely paranoid, and being brought in involuntarily by police. When well he is capable, works part-time, and consistently states while an inpatient that he does not believe he has an illness and will stop medication as soon as he is discharged.

He is now nearing discharge from the current admission, is settled on paliperidone depot, and the treating team is considering a community treatment order.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no active psychotic symptoms, insight limited into illness.

lead_in: Which combination of features most strongly supports proceeding with a community treatment order?

options.text: The treating team's shared concern that he will disengage from all community services soon after this discharge
options.rationale: Inpatient status does not automatically convert to a CTO; a separate assessment against CTO-specific criteria and review is required. Would conflate two orders. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

options.text: The family's request that his medication be legally enforced so that the household feels safe living with him again
options.rationale: Clinician concern alone does not satisfy statutory criteria; the Act requires evidence of prior pattern and lack of less-restrictive alternative. Would be legally insufficient. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: His limited insight into having a chronic mental illness while he is on the ward this admission and previously
options.rationale: Family preference is not a statutory ground; the Act protects the individual under specified criteria, not the wishes of relatives. Would misground the order. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

options.text: His current involuntary inpatient status justifying automatic continuation of the same order into the community setting
options.rationale: Poor insight is common and is not a stand-alone criterion for a CTO; it must be tied to a demonstrated relapse-on-cessation pattern. Would be relevant context but not the basis. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Documented relapse pattern on cessation, prior benefit from treatment, and no less-restrictive alternative to prevent deterioration
options.rationale: State Mental Health Acts require that a CTO be based on a demonstrated pattern showing the person is likely to stop treatment and deteriorate, that treatment has previously benefited them, and that no less-restrictive means (e.g. voluntary depot with case-management) would suffice. All three limbs must be present; this patient meets them. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007 s 51; Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

explanation.summary: CTOs are outpatient treatment orders authorised only where a demonstrated pattern of relapse on treatment cessation, previous treatment benefit, and lack of a less-restrictive alternative are all established. They are subject to periodic review by an independent tribunal.
key_points: CTO requires all three limbs, not clinician concern alone
Poor insight is context, not a stand-alone ground
Family preference does not ground an order
Inpatient status does not auto-convert to a CTO
Independent tribunal review is a statutory safeguard
explanation.pearls: A CTO is a serious intrusion on liberty and must be reviewed; teams should reassess whether the least-restrictive threshold still holds at each renewal.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

stem:
You are asked to see a 41-year-old man in custody who has been charged with a serious assault. His solicitor has raised concerns about his ability to participate in proceedings. He has a background of chronic schizophrenia with residual negative symptoms, is currently stable on clozapine, and denies acute psychotic symptoms. On interview he can name his solicitor, states the charge against him accurately, and describes what happened at the alleged incident coherently.

However, when you explore his understanding of court process he tells you he thinks the magistrate is 'like a referee' who will 'decide who wins the argument', and that if he pleads not guilty the jury will vote about whether they believe him or the victim, without being able to describe the role of evidence, cross-examination or the meaning of a guilty plea.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no thought disorder, no active hallucinations or delusions.

lead_in: Which is the most accurate conclusion regarding his fitness to stand trial under Australian common-law criteria?

options.text: He is likely unfit because he cannot follow proceedings or grasp the substantial effect of evidence given against him
options.rationale: The Australian common-law Presser criteria (R v Presser 1958) test the accused's ability to: understand the nature of the charge, plead, exercise the right of challenge, understand the nature of the proceedings, follow the course of the proceedings, understand the substantial effect of any evidence given against him, and communicate a defence to counsel. Understanding the charge and having a memory of events does not satisfy the wider list; inability to grasp evidence and procedure is a classic Presser failure. (Source: R v Presser [1958] VR 45; RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

options.text: He is fit because he can state the charge accurately and gives a coherent factual account of the alleged incident
options.rationale: Presser fitness is a multi-limbed functional test; charge-recall and factual memory are two of several limbs and are not sufficient in isolation. Would misapply the test. (Source: R v Presser [1958] VR 45).

options.text: He is fit because he is not currently floridly psychotic and is clinically stable on his maintenance clozapine treatment
options.rationale: Fitness is functional and case-specific, not driven by symptom status. Residual cognitive or negative symptoms can render an otherwise stable patient unfit. Would confuse clinical stability with legal fitness. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

options.text: He is fit because the defence of insanity applies only to the accused's mental state at the time of the offence
options.rationale: This confuses fitness to stand trial (present-time capacity to participate) with the McNaghten defence (state at the time of the alleged offence). They are separate doctrines. Would conflate two questions. (Source: R v Presser [1958] VR 45; McNaghten's Case (1843) 8 ER 718).

options.text: The fitness question is for the treating psychiatrist alone to determine at the next multidisciplinary team meeting
options.rationale: Fitness is determined by the court on the balance of probabilities; the psychiatrist provides expert opinion but does not decide. Would misattribute the decision. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

explanation.summary: The Presser test asks whether the accused can meaningfully participate in trial across seven limbs. Failing any single limb (e.g. inability to understand the effect of evidence) can render a person unfit despite an intact factual account. Fitness and the insanity defence are separate.
key_points: Presser is a multi-limbed functional test
Fitness is time-of-trial; McNaghten is time-of-offence
Residual negative symptoms can drive unfitness even when stable
The court decides on balance of probabilities
Psychiatrist provides expert opinion, not the verdict
explanation.pearls: Charge-recall is not evidence-understanding. Testing all Presser limbs functionally is essential in a serious matter.

stem:
A 39-year-old man with a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder, chronic methamphetamine use, and one prior conviction for assault is being reviewed after admission for suicidal ideation. Before discharge you are asked to document a violence-risk assessment. You have access to his full history, the collateral from partner and probation, an actuarial risk instrument scored by the on-call registrar, and a structured professional-judgement schedule (HCR-20 v3).

The registrar is asking which framework should carry most weight when you formulate risk and communicate it to the treating team.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no active psychotic symptoms; irritable affect.
data_table.Investigations: UDS positive for methamphetamine; bloods within normal limits.

lead_in: Which approach is most appropriate to guide clinical decision-making here?

options.text: Rely on the actuarial score alone because it yields a numerical probability that is easily communicated to the team
options.rationale: Actuarial tools give group-level probabilities and do not identify dynamic modifiable factors for management. Would produce a false-precision output without a management plan. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

options.text: Use structured professional judgement (HCR-20 v3) integrating historical, clinical and risk-management items, and formulate
options.rationale: Structured professional judgement (SPJ) instruments such as the HCR-20 v3 combine empirically-derived risk factors with individualised formulation and identify dynamic factors amenable to management. In clinical settings SPJ outperforms unstructured judgement and produces actionable case-specific plans, unlike actuarial tools which yield probabilistic group-level estimates. RANZCP forensic guidance supports SPJ as the primary framework for clinical risk. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance; Douglas et al HCR-20 v3 manual).

options.text: Use unstructured clinical judgement based on your overall impression of the patient after your interview with him today
options.rationale: Unstructured judgement has the weakest evidence for accuracy and is prone to bias. Would be inferior to SPJ. (Source: HCR-20 v3 manual).

options.text: Assign him to a categorical low, medium or high risk band as the primary output for the discharge documentation
options.rationale: Categorical banding without formulation is deprecated in Australian practice for the same reasons it is in suicide risk work: it creates false reassurance and does not drive management. Would be a discouraged pattern. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

options.text: Decline to produce a risk assessment because violence prediction has poor accuracy at the level of the individual patient
options.rationale: The limits of prediction do not release clinicians from the duty to assess and manage; the response is to use the best available structured method with humility about accuracy, not to abstain. Would abrogate duty of care. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

explanation.summary: Structured professional judgement is the current standard for clinical violence-risk assessment because it identifies dynamic factors and drives management. Actuarial tools have a role but do not replace formulation, and unstructured judgement is the least defensible approach.
key_points: SPJ integrates empirical risk items with individual formulation
Actuarial tools give group-level, not case-specific, output
Unstructured judgement performs worst and is bias-prone
Categorical banding is deprecated in modern AU practice
Prediction is imperfect but abstention is not the answer
explanation.pearls: The point of risk assessment is to change what happens next, not to produce a number.

stem:
A 24-year-old man on a state Mental Health Act assessment order in the ED has become acutely agitated. Verbal de-escalation over 20 minutes and offered oral olanzapine have both failed. He is pacing, punching walls and has now threatened staff. He has not eaten today. The clinical team must act to prevent injury to himself and others.

He has no known cardiac history, no relevant drug allergies, and a code black team has arrived.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, tachycardic, no evidence of head injury or intoxication other than clinical impression.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step consistent with least-restrictive-practice principles?

options.text: Apply mechanical restraint for the rest of the shift so that the team can safely monitor him from a distance in seclusion
options.rationale: De-escalation has already been tried and failed and there is now imminent risk of injury; persisting alone abandons duty to protect. Would be unsafe. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement 61).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

options.text: Continue verbal de-escalation without further medication as escalation is a nursing rather than a medical issue tonight
options.rationale: Mechanical restraint is a last resort with strict time-limited use and one-to-one nursing; a whole shift of mechanical restraint is disproportionate when parenteral sedation can achieve control faster and less intrusively. Would breach least-restrictive practice. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement 61).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

options.text: Administer parenteral sedation as chemical restraint with the smallest safe team, monitoring vitals and airway continuously
options.rationale: The least-restrictive principle in acute behavioural emergencies favours the option that achieves control with the least prolonged intrusion. Once verbal de-escalation and oral medication have failed, parenteral chemical sedation (e.g. IM droperidol or IM olanzapine per state guidelines) with monitoring is generally preferred over prolonged mechanical restraint. Mechanical restraint is a last resort with strict monitoring and time limits. (Source: NSW Health Aggression, Seclusion and Restraint in Mental Health Facilities Guideline; RANZCP Position Statement 61 on Restraint).
source_refs: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline
RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

options.text: Call police to remove him from the department under public-order offences and transfer him into the local watch-house
options.rationale: He is a detained patient under the Act with an apparent mental disorder; transferring him to police custody is neither clinically indicated nor lawful for a mental-health emergency in a health facility. Would misroute care. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

options.text: Give a large stat oral benzodiazepine dose despite prior oral refusal to try to achieve chemical control non-parenterally
options.rationale: Oral administration has already been refused and behavioural escalation is beyond the reliability of oral therapy; ignoring that refusal to force-feed oral medication is neither safe nor lawful. Would be inappropriate route. (Source: NSW Health Aggression Guideline).
source_refs: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline

explanation.summary: The restraint hierarchy in Australian mental health settings runs from verbal de-escalation to offered oral medication to parenteral chemical restraint, with mechanical restraint and seclusion as options of last resort under strict monitoring. Least-restrictive-practice principles govern the escalation.
key_points: De-escalation and oral medication are first steps
Parenteral chemical restraint precedes mechanical restraint
Mechanical restraint requires 1:1 nursing and strict time limits
Ongoing physical and physiological monitoring is mandatory
Post-event debrief with patient and staff is required
explanation.pearls: Every restrictive-practice episode is a reportable safety event and should trigger review of preventable antecedents.

sources.label: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline
RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

stem: A 30-year-old woman on an inpatient psychiatric unit has been placed in seclusion after a serious assault on a nurse. She is under a state Mental Health Act treatment order. The consultant psychiatrist has authorised the seclusion order and documented the indication. You are the medical registrar covering the ward that evening.

data_table.Examination: Post-medication, drowsy but rousable, breathing normally.
data_table.Investigations: Vitals recorded pre-seclusion within normal limits.

lead_in: Which set of monitoring requirements is most consistent with Australian standards for a seclusion episode?

options.text: Check on the patient at the start of the shift and again at the end of the shift with a documented mental state note
options.rationale: Time-limited seclusion demands medical review within specified short intervals to reassess necessity, not deferral until the next round. Would violate the review interval. (Source: NSW Health Aggression Guideline).
source_refs: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline

options.text: Use continuous CCTV monitoring without in-person checks in order to minimise staff exposure during the seclusion event
options.rationale: Intermittent checks miss deterioration during a period of high physical and psychological risk. Would breach monitoring standards. (Source: NSW Health Aggression Guideline).
source_refs: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline

options.text: Have medical review only at the next scheduled ward round on the following morning, with nursing observations overnight
options.rationale: CCTV supplements but does not replace in-person monitoring; deteriorating airway, occult injury or physical health deterioration are not reliably detected on camera. Would be inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement 61).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

options.text: Continuous visual observation with regular physical and mental-state checks, timely medical review, and release considered each review
options.rationale: Australian standards (NSW Health, National Standards for Mental Health Services, RANZCP Position Statement 61) require continuous visual observation of the person in seclusion, regular documented physical and mental-state checks (typically every 10-15 minutes), medical review within jurisdiction-specified intervals, and active consideration of release at each review. Seclusion is time-limited and must end at the earliest safe opportunity. (Source: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline; RANZCP Position Statement 61).
source_refs: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline
RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

options.text: Release the patient at the end of the standard four-hour block regardless of ongoing clinical need or risk to staff
options.rationale: Seclusion must be ended at the earliest safe opportunity but continued only where clinically necessary and re-authorised; automatic release irrespective of clinical state is not a safe rule. Would be arbitrary. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement 61).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

explanation.summary: Seclusion is a highly restrictive intervention with strict monitoring, review, documentation and debrief requirements. Standards require continuous visual observation, regular in-person checks, timely medical review, active consideration of release, and post-event review.
key_points: Continuous visual observation with regular in-person checks
Medical review within jurisdiction-specific intervals
Active consideration of release at each review
CCTV supplements but does not replace in-person checks
Post-event debrief with patient and staff is required
explanation.pearls: Every seclusion event is a KPI: services track and aim to reduce total time in seclusion.

sources.label: NSW Health Aggression Seclusion and Restraint Guideline
RANZCP Position Statement 61 Minimising Restrictive Practices

stem:
A 34-year-old woman brings her 3-year-old son to your GP clinic for review of a rash. During the consultation she becomes tearful and discloses that her partner has been drinking heavily, has been hitting her, and last week grabbed the child roughly and left a bruise on his upper arm. She does not want to involve authorities, and asks you to keep the disclosure confidential.

On examination the child has an oval bruise on the medial upper arm consistent with a grip mark. She agrees to a domestic violence phone service referral.

data_table.Examination: Child alert, well-grown, oval bruise medial right upper arm; no other injuries noted.

lead_in: What is your obligation regarding the child?

options.text: Respect her stated request for confidentiality and document a plan to reassess the situation at the next scheduled clinic visit
options.rationale: A police report of adult DV does not discharge the specific mandatory reporting obligation to child protection; both may be indicated, but reporting to the child protection agency for the child is the specific duty here. Would omit the required pathway. (Source: state Care and Protection Acts).
source_refs: NSW Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998

options.text: Report only if she consents to disclosure after further counselling in a dedicated follow-up appointment later this week
options.rationale: Confidentiality does not override statutory mandatory reporting obligations for suspected child abuse; deferring risks further harm. Would breach the reporting duty. (Source: AIFS Mandatory Reporting Resource Sheet).

options.text: Refer to the paediatrician you know at the local hospital and ask them to make the report on your behalf next week
options.rationale: Reporting is not conditional on parental consent and delay to obtain it is not permitted. Would misconceive the duty. (Source: state Care and Protection Acts).
source_refs: NSW Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998

options.text: Report the partner directly to police for assault instead of contacting the state child protection agency about the child
options.rationale: The mandatory reporter who forms the reasonable belief is the person who must report; the duty is personal and cannot be delegated to a later clinician. Would displace responsibility. (Source: AIFS Mandatory Reporting Resource Sheet).

options.text: Make a mandatory report to the state child protection agency given a reasonable belief of significant harm to the child
options.rationale: All Australian states and territories make medical practitioners mandatory reporters for suspected child physical abuse. The threshold is a reasonable belief (not certainty) that the child has been or is at risk of significant harm. Mother's request for confidentiality does not override the statutory obligation, though it should inform how disclosure is handled and the family supported afterwards. (Source: AIFS Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse and Neglect resource sheet; state Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Acts).
source_refs: NSW Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998

explanation.summary: Mandatory reporting for suspected child abuse applies to medical practitioners in every Australian state and territory. The threshold is reasonable belief of significant harm and the obligation is not overridden by parental refusal. The specific pathway is the state child protection agency.
key_points: Reasonable belief, not certainty, is the threshold
Parental refusal does not remove the obligation
The reporter who forms the belief must report
Police report is separate from child protection report
Family support and DV referral remain part of good care
explanation.pearls: Documenting the reasonable-belief basis in the notes is important legal and clinical practice.

sources.label: NSW Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998

stem:
A 46-year-old man attends his second session with you in a community mental health clinic. He has depression and long-standing conflict with a specific former business partner. He tells you today that he has bought a specific firearm, has looked up his former partner's address, and describes a detailed plan to shoot him next weekend when the former partner is expected to be at his home. He says he is only telling you because he wanted 'someone to know'.

He explicitly asks that this remain confidential and threatens to end therapy if you break confidence. He has capacity for this discussion.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect constricted, no psychotic features.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Breach confidentiality by warning police and the intended victim, then arrange urgent psychiatric assessment for detention
options.rationale: Australian medical confidentiality is not absolute and privacy legislation (Privacy Act 1988 APP 6, state health privacy Acts) permits disclosure without consent where there is a serious and imminent threat to the life or health of another person. Where the threat meets that threshold - identifiable victim, means, plan, and time frame - the treating clinician is expected to warn police and if possible the victim, alongside arranging urgent psychiatric assessment. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics 2018; Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) APP 6; MDA National / Avant guidance on duty to warn).
source_refs: MDA National / Avant duty to warn guidance

options.text: Maintain confidentiality on the basis that no such duty to warn a third party exists in current Australian medical practice
options.rationale: Australia does not have a general common-law duty to warn identical to the US Tarasoff decision, but privacy legislation, professional codes, and the specific threshold of serious and imminent threat permit and effectively require disclosure. Would be a legal and ethical failure. (Source: MDA National / Avant guidance).
source_refs: MDA National / Avant duty to warn guidance

options.text: Ask him to sign a written no-harm contract and continue outpatient treatment with weekly review by yourself at the clinic
options.rationale: No-harm contracts have no evidence base and cannot address an articulated plan with means, victim and time frame. Would abandon the third party at risk. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

options.text: Warn only the intended victim and not the police in order to preserve as much of the therapeutic confidentiality as possible
options.rationale: Where there is a threat to life the appropriate agency to prevent the harm is generally police; warning only the victim without means of protection is inadequate. Would misroute the warning. (Source: MDA National / Avant guidance).
source_refs: MDA National / Avant duty to warn guidance

options.text: Formally terminate the therapy relationship today so that you no longer have a treating clinician's duty to act on the disclosure
options.rationale: Terminating therapy does not extinguish the ethical or legal position; information about a serious and imminent threat already known must still be acted on. Would be an evasion. (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).

explanation.summary: Australia relies on privacy law, professional codes and civil liability rather than a Tarasoff-style common-law duty, but where a threat is serious and imminent and directed at an identifiable person, disclosure to police and the victim is both permitted and expected, alongside urgent psychiatric assessment.
key_points: Serious and imminent threat is the disclosure threshold
Warn police first; consider warning the victim
Arrange urgent psychiatric assessment in parallel
No-harm contracts have no evidence base
Terminating therapy does not extinguish the duty
explanation.pearls: Document the reasoning that led you to conclude the threshold was met; medico-legal insurers expect a clear contemporaneous record.

sources.label: MDA National / Avant duty to warn guidance

stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends your GP clinic alone requesting a prescription for the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has been in a sexual relationship for 4 months with her 16-year-old partner. On assessment she can describe how the pill works, the main side-effect profile including VTE risk, the requirement for daily dosing, and the option of condoms for STI protection. She has thought about whether to tell her parents and prefers not to.

She has no medical contraindications and safeguarding screening (HEADSSS) does not raise any concerns about the relationship being non-consensual.
lead_in: Which principle most correctly guides your decision on whether to prescribe?

options.text: Refuse to prescribe without parental consent because she is under 16 years of age and cannot lawfully consent alone
options.rationale: There is no fixed age below which a minor cannot consent; the Mature Minor doctrine applies from any age at which competence for the specific decision can be demonstrated. Would misstate the law. (Source: Marion's Case).

options.text: Assess her Gillick competence for this decision, including understanding of the treatment and implications, and prescribe if competent
options.rationale: The High Court in Marion's Case adopted the Gillick / Mature Minor principle: a person under 18 can consent to medical treatment without parental involvement if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence to understand the nature and consequences of the proposed treatment. Assessment is decision-specific. Contraception for a competent 15-year-old in a consensual relationship falls within this framework, provided safeguarding is addressed. (Source: Secretary DHCS v JWB and SMB (Marion's Case) (1992) 175 CLR 218; RACGP guidance on adolescent care).

options.text: Contact her parents against her stated wishes today to obtain parental consent for the combined oral contraceptive pill
options.rationale: Where the minor is competent, unilaterally contacting parents breaches confidentiality and the doctor-patient relationship. Would be inappropriate. (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health).

options.text: Report the sexual relationship to police because she is a minor engaged in a sexual relationship with a peer of similar age
options.rationale: The Australian age of consent varies by state but a consensual peer relationship in this age range is generally not a mandatory reporting matter unless safeguarding concerns are identified; blanket reporting would breach confidentiality and misapply the law. Would be a category error. (Source: state Crimes Acts and RACGP guidance).

options.text: Defer prescribing until she returns to the clinic with a parent for a joint follow-up consultation to discuss contraception
options.rationale: Deferral for parental attendance when the minor is competent is not required, and creates a barrier that increases risk of unintended pregnancy. Would be paternalistic and clinically inferior. (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health).

explanation.summary: The Mature Minor / Gillick doctrine in Australia allows competent minors to consent to treatment without parental involvement. Assessment is decision-specific, considers understanding and safeguarding, and does not turn on a fixed age.
key_points: Competence is decision-specific, not age-fixed
Understanding of treatment and its implications is the test
Safeguarding screening is a separate but necessary step
Parental contact against wishes breaches confidentiality
Deferring competent care increases clinical risk
explanation.pearls: Documenting the competence assessment and what safeguarding was addressed is essential in the record.

stem:
You are the GP for an 82-year-old woman living in a Commonwealth-funded residential aged care facility. She has moderate Alzheimer disease and periodically loses capacity for complex decisions. Her son (financial enduring power of attorney) has been observed by staff shouting at her repeatedly during visits, and a bruise pattern on her forearm was noted at last week's shower. She tells you today, when he is not present, that she is 'scared when he visits'. She does not want you to do anything.

Her capacity for this specific decision (about reporting) is impaired; she cannot describe options for action, or weigh the implications of reporting or not reporting.

data_table.Examination: Frail, resolving bruise linear pattern medial left forearm; MoCA previously 14/30.
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coags within normal limits.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Respect her stated wish that no action be taken and document the conversation, arranging closer nursing observation and review
options.rationale: Direct confrontation without safeguarding action can escalate risk; the correct approach is systemic reporting with support from the safeguarding framework, not a private conversation. Would be unsafe. (Source: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS).
source_refs: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS

options.text: Confront the son directly and demand that he stop the behaviour before contemplating any formal safeguarding or agency report
options.rationale: Her capacity for this decision is impaired, so her stated wish does not carry the same weight as a competent refusal; she also does not have the practical capacity to protect herself from further abuse. Would abandon safeguarding duty. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987).

options.text: Report through the Serious Incident Response Scheme via the facility and consider notifying the Public Advocate given impaired capacity
options.rationale: The Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission's Serious Incident Response Scheme (SIRS) requires providers to report reportable incidents (which include unlawful sexual contact, physical assault, psychological or emotional abuse, unexplained absence and unexpected death) affecting residents. GPs working with the facility should escalate through SIRS and consider referral to the state Public Advocate or Guardianship Tribunal where the person cannot protect their own interests. Her refusal does not override the safeguarding obligation because capacity for this decision is impaired. (Source: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS; state Guardianship Act; Australian Human Rights Commission Elder Abuse resources).
source_refs: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS

options.text: Report the son directly to police as the only channel available for adult abuse in a Commonwealth-funded aged-care setting
options.rationale: Police may become involved but the specific aged-care safeguarding scheme (SIRS) and the state guardianship pathway address the specific setting and financial and personal welfare implications, and are the appropriate primary channels. Would miss the aged-care specific framework. (Source: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS).
source_refs: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS

options.text: Ask the facility to restrict his visits informally without any formal report to a safeguarding agency or state authority
options.rationale: Informal restriction without a lawful pathway (guardianship, protection order) is legally unsupported and risks challenge; formal reporting and guardianship engagement is the correct route. Would be legally unsound. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987).

explanation.summary: Elder abuse in residential aged care in Australia is addressed through SIRS reporting by providers, referral to the state Public Advocate or Guardianship Tribunal where the person's capacity is impaired, and consideration of police involvement for criminal acts. GPs have a role in escalating and documenting.
key_points: SIRS covers physical, psychological and other categories of abuse
Impaired capacity changes the weight of refusal to report
State guardianship pathway addresses substitute decision-making
Direct confrontation without safeguarding can escalate risk
Documentation of the reasoning is essential
explanation.pearls: Financial abuse by an EPOA is a common pattern; consider requesting review of the enduring power of attorney via the state tribunal.

sources.label: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission SIRS

subtopic_detail: Advance statements and Mental Health Act
stem:
A 38-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder and prior severe manic episodes has completed a psychiatric advance statement while well and had it witnessed appropriately. In it she specifies that during manic relapses she prefers oral quetiapine, refuses lithium (which she previously found intolerable), and requests that her sister be contacted as her nominated support person before any treatment decisions.

She now re-presents in the ED in an acute manic episode. She lacks capacity, is under a state Mental Health Act assessment order, and the treating psychiatrist is deciding on treatment. Both quetiapine and lithium are clinically reasonable options.

data_table.Examination: Elevated mood, pressured speech, mildly disorganised.

lead_in: How should her advance statement most appropriately be handled?

options.text: Disregard the advance statement now because she currently lacks capacity to reaffirm the preferences that were previously recorded
options.rationale: Where both agents are clinically reasonable, guideline-first-line status does not justify overriding a valid advance statement; departures require justification specific to the case, not general practice. Would breach the statutory duty. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

options.text: Follow the advance statement only if her sister as nominated support person agrees in advance to every specific element in it
options.rationale: Advance statements are designed precisely for periods of incapacity; disregarding them because capacity is now lost defeats their purpose and is inconsistent with the current Acts. Would misunderstand the instrument. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022

options.text: Override the statement by preferring lithium because it is a standard first-line agent recommended in bipolar treatment guidelines
options.rationale: The nominated support person's role is to help communicate the person's will and preferences, not to veto the advance statement. Would misconceive the support role. (Source: RANZCP Position on Supported Decision Making).
source_refs: RANZCP Position on Supported Decision Making

options.text: Prescribe quetiapine per her advance statement and contact her nominated support person, documenting reasons if any element cannot be followed
options.rationale: Modern state Mental Health Acts (notably Victoria and Queensland) require the treating team to give effect to a person's advance statement wherever it is clinically reasonable to do so, and to consult the nominated support person. Departures must be justified and documented. Where both listed options (quetiapine and lithium) are clinically reasonable, the advance statement resolves the choice in favour of the patient's expressed preference. (Source: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022; RANZCP Position on Supported Decision Making).
source_refs: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022
RANZCP Position on Supported Decision Making

options.text: Defer any medication now until she regains capacity to reconsider her preferences and provide fresh contemporaneous informed consent
options.rationale: Deferring effective treatment during acute mania causes ongoing harm and undermines the purpose of the advance statement; the statement guides current care. Would be inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP CPG Bipolar).

explanation.summary: Psychiatric advance statements are recognised in several Australian state Acts and are intended to be followed during periods of incapacity where clinically reasonable. Nominated support persons help communicate the person's preferences but do not veto them. Overrides require case-specific justification.
key_points: Advance statements activate during incapacity
Clinically reasonable elements should be followed
Nominated support person is a communicator, not a veto-holder
Departures must be documented with case-specific reasons
Standard first-line status is not itself a reason to override
explanation.pearls: Reviewing the advance statement with the patient while well after each admission strengthens its future usefulness.

sources.label: Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022
RANZCP Position on Supported Decision Making

stem:
An 84-year-old woman is admitted with a displaced intracapsular hip fracture. The orthopaedic team recommends hip hemiarthroplasty within 48 hours. When you assess her at 09:00 she is oriented, understands the operation and the risks of anaesthesia, and agrees to proceed. At 17:00 the ward calls: she is now confused, pulling at her drip, telling nurses she wants to go home to feed her cat (she has no cat), and is refusing surgery loudly. She has fluctuating attention, is easily distracted, and cannot follow a three-step command. Nothing is documented about her earlier capacity assessment beyond a brief operative consent form she signed at 09:00.

She has no formal enduring guardian. Her daughter (next of kin) is contactable and was not present for either conversation. Surgery within the next 24 hours reduces her mortality risk substantially.

data_table.Examination: At 09:00 alert, oriented; at 17:00 4AT score 8, inattentive, mildly hyperactive delirium.
data_table.Investigations: UEC and inflammatory markers pending; UA leukocytes and nitrites positive.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to consent for surgery now?

options.text: Accept the current refusal as valid because it is the most recent expressed preference recorded from the patient this admission
options.rationale: Hip-fracture mortality rises with surgical delay and delirium may not resolve promptly; passive waiting is not compatible with the ANZSGM standards for early surgery and disrespects the earlier capacitous decision. Would harm the patient. (Source: ANZSGM hip fracture position).
source_refs: ANZSGM position on hip fracture care

options.text: Apply urgently to the state Guardianship Tribunal for an emergency guardian to consent to surgery before proceeding with the operation
options.rationale: A refusal made without capacity is not a valid refusal; the most-recent-preference rule applies only between capacitous expressions. Would incorrectly weight the delirious statement over the capacitous one. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines).

options.text: Proceed under the emergency common-law doctrine of necessity, ignoring the earlier capacitous consent that was signed at 09:00 today
options.rationale: Tribunal application is appropriate where no less-formal pathway exists and the decision is contested, but where an earlier capacitous consent exists and the person responsible under statute can be engaged for corroboration, urgent tribunal is disproportionate for this common scenario. Would be over-escalated. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987).

options.text: Wait until she is fully lucid and no longer delirious before proceeding with surgery, regardless of how long the recovery takes
options.rationale: Necessity applies only when a valid consent cannot be obtained and treatment cannot wait; a valid capacitous consent already exists, so relying on necessity is legally weaker and unnecessary. Would misuse the doctrine. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines).

options.text: Rely on the earlier capacitous consent as it was given for this operation while she had capacity, and consult daughter as person responsible
options.rationale: Australian consent law recognises that a consent validly given while a person had capacity for the specific decision remains operative for that decision unless withdrawn while capacitous. Her current refusal is made without capacity and cannot itself withdraw the earlier valid consent, though the team must actively work to restore her capacity (treat delirium, treat UTI) and consult the person responsible under state guardianship legislation to ratify or refine the plan. Deferral of surgery carries substantial mortality cost that the earlier capacitous decision has already weighed. (Source: NHMRC Consent Guidelines; NSW Guardianship Act 1987; ANZSGM position on hip fracture care).
source_refs: ANZSGM position on hip fracture care

explanation.summary: A valid capacitous consent remains operative unless withdrawn while capacitous. Fluctuating capacity from delirium requires active treatment of the delirium and engagement of the statutory person responsible, but does not invalidate the prior capacitous decision. Necessity and tribunal applications are pathways for when no valid consent exists.
key_points: Capacitous consent survives loss of capacity for that decision
A non-capacitous refusal cannot withdraw a valid consent
Actively treat and reassess the delirium in parallel
Person responsible under state statute is the immediate ally
Tribunal and necessity are last-resort routes when no valid consent exists
explanation.pearls: Detailed documentation of the earlier capacity assessment at the time of the operative consent is the single most protective clinical practice for this common scenario.

sources.label: ANZSGM position on hip fracture care

stem:
You are asked to write an expert report on a 33-year-old man charged with the serious assault of his neighbour. At the time of the offence he had untreated schizophrenia with a fixed delusion that the neighbour was a government operative sent to kill his family. He believed he was defending his children pre-emptively. Interviews after treatment reveal that he had a coherent understanding of the physical nature of the act (that punching would cause injury), and knew that ordinarily punching a person would be legally wrong, but believed at the time that his specific act was morally right because it was necessary to save his family from imminent harm.

His chronic schizophrenia is well documented, contemporaneous ambulance and police records describe florid psychosis at the scene, and there is no evidence of intoxication.

data_table.Examination: Now stabilised on clozapine, insight into past psychosis intact.

lead_in: Which formulation most correctly applies the mental impairment defence in this case?

options.text: The defence fails because he knew that punching a person is generally illegal and this satisfies the legal wrongness limb entirely
options.rationale: Presence of psychosis does not automatically satisfy the defence; the specific limbs (nature and quality OR wrongness) must be engaged by the psychosis in the specific act. Would over-generalise the defence. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

options.text: The defence succeeds automatically because he was documented as psychotic at the time of the alleged assault on the neighbour
options.rationale: Stapleton v R held that in Australia the wrongness limb is moral wrongness, not merely legal wrongness. Would apply the wrong test. (Source: Stapleton v R (1952) 86 CLR 358).

options.text: He may satisfy the wrongness limb because a delusion making him believe the act was morally right can defeat knowledge of wrongness
options.rationale: The McNaghten rules and their Australian statutory equivalents (e.g. Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) s 7.3; Victorian Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997) provide a defence where, because of a mental impairment, the accused did not know the nature and quality of the act OR did not know it was wrong. Australian authority (Stapleton v R (1952) 86 CLR 358) clarifies that 'wrong' means morally wrong according to the standards of reasonable people, not merely legally wrong. A delusion producing a genuine belief that the specific act was morally right can therefore satisfy the wrongness limb even where general legal knowledge is intact. (Source: Stapleton v R (1952) 86 CLR 358; Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) s 7.3; RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

options.text: The defence turns on his current mental state on clozapine rather than his mental state at the time of the alleged offence itself
options.rationale: The mental impairment defence assesses the accused's state at the time of the offence; current state is the domain of fitness to stand trial. Would conflate two doctrines. (Source: R v Presser [1958] VR 45; Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) s 7.3).

options.text: The defence is exclusively a matter for the treating psychiatrist and cannot be independently evaluated by an expert court reporter
options.rationale: The mental impairment defence is decided by the court on expert opinion; the expert reporter provides opinion, the treating psychiatrist has a separate role, and neither decides the defence. Would misallocate the decision. (Source: RANZCP Forensic Faculty guidance).

explanation.summary: The Australian mental impairment defence descends from McNaghten and is codified in Commonwealth and state law. The wrongness limb is moral wrongness per Stapleton v R, not merely legal wrongness. A delusion that convinced the accused the specific act was morally justified can satisfy this limb even where general legal knowledge is intact.
key_points: Two limbs: nature and quality OR wrongness
Wrongness is moral wrongness (Stapleton v R)
Psychosis alone is not automatic; the limbs must be engaged
State at time of offence, not present state
Court decides on expert opinion; the expert opines, not decides
explanation.pearls: Contemporaneous ambulance, police and witness records describing the mental state at the scene are often decisive in reconstructing the state at the time of the act.
